etymology: American missionary (1718-1747) to the Indians of New England, whose diary, published by Jonathan Edwards, has stirred missions for centuries.
biblical_def: David Brainerd was a young American missionary to the Native Americans of the colonial frontier, whose brief, suffering, prayer-soaked life has influenced the cause of missions out of all proportion to its length. Expelled from Yale for an unguarded remark during the Great Awakening, he gave himself to the gospel among the Delaware Indians of New Jersey and Pennsylvania, riding through wilderness, sleeping on straw, wracked by the tuberculosis that would kill him at twenty-nine. He saw a genuine work of God's Spirit among the Indians, and recorded his labors, agonies, and seasons of communion with God in a journal of remarkable depth. After his death in the home of Jonathan Edwards, nursed by Edwards's daughter Jerusha, Edwards published The Life and Diary of David Brainerd, which became one of the most influential devotional and missionary books ever written, moving William Carey, Henry Martyn, Adoniram Judson, and countless others to the field. Brainerd stands in the dictionary as the consumptive young missionary whose diary kindled the modern missionary movement, who taught the church by his example that a short life poured out in prayer and labor for the lost is no waste, but a seed that bears fruit for generations.
webster_summary: American missionary (1718-1747) to the Delaware Indians, dead of tuberculosis at twenty-nine; his diary, published by Jonathan Edwards, became one of the most influential missionary books ever, stirring Carey, Martyn, and Judson to the field.

corruption_summary: Brainerd's life honors the recovery of prayerful, sacrificial missions and the truth that a short life spent for Christ is no waste, against a comfort-seeking religion that counts such sacrifice as folly.
corruption_paragraphs: Comfort-religion correction. A self-protective Christianity counts Brainerd's wilderness sufferings and early death a tragic waste. The gospel reckons otherwise: except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abides alone, but in dying it brings forth much fruit (John 12:24). The dictionary holds that a life poured out for Christ and the lost, however brief, is fruitful beyond reckoning; Brainerd's twenty-nine years still feed the missionary zeal of the church centuries on.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the priority of secret prayer in the work of God. Brainerd's diary records hours of wrestling with God in the woods, and it was prayer, more than method, that marked his fruitful seasons. The dictionary commends his example: the advance of the gospel is born in the closet of prayer, and the church that would see the Spirit work among the nations must first labor, as Brainerd did, on its knees.

etymology: First American foreign missionary (1788-1850), pioneer to Burma and translator of the Burmese Bible.
biblical_def: Adoniram Judson was the first American foreign missionary, the pioneer of the gospel in Burma, and one of the great sufferers in the history of missions. Sent out in 1812, he and his wife Ann labored for years before seeing a single convert, learning the Burmese language and translating the Scriptures. Judson gave his life to rendering the whole Bible into Burmese, a labor of decades that remains the standard translation among Burmese Christians to this day. His path was marked by terrible affliction: imprisonment for nearly two years in the death-prison of Ava during war, chained and tormented; the deaths of two wives and several children; recurring sickness and grief that drove him at times to the edge of despair. Yet he pressed on, and from his perseverance came a thriving Burmese church, especially among the Karen people, that endures and grows to this day. Judson stands in the dictionary as the suffering pioneer of Burma, who counted no anguish too great to give the Scriptures and the gospel to a people without Christ, and whose labors, watered with tears and blood, brought forth a harvest that has outlasted his every sorrow.
webster_summary: First American foreign missionary (1788-1850), pioneer to Burma and translator of the Burmese Bible; who through imprisonment, the loss of wives and children, and years without converts laid the foundation of an enduring Burmese church.

corruption_paragraphs: Pluralism correction. A modern pluralism insists that the nations have their own religions and need not the gospel of Christ, making missions an arrogant intrusion. Judson's life answers from Scripture: how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard (Rom 10:14)? The dictionary holds the necessity and exclusivity of Christ — there is salvation in no other name — and commends the missionary's conviction that the unreached must hear, whatever the cost to the messenger.

This entry faces little further postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is perseverance through suffering and delay. Judson labored years without a convert, buried wives and children, and endured the horrors of Ava's prison, yet did not quit. The dictionary commends his steadfastness: those who sow the precious seed in tears shall doubtless come again rejoicing, bringing their sheaves (Psa 126:6). The Burmese church today is the harvest of his refusal to give up.

etymology: English missionary and Bible translator (1781-1812) to India and Persia, who resolved to "burn out for God."
biblical_def: Henry Martyn was an English missionary and translator of brilliant gifts and consuming zeal, who gave his short life to carrying the Scriptures to the peoples of India and Persia. A scholar of the first rank at Cambridge, he turned from a promising academic career to the mission field, sailing to India as a chaplain, with the words on his heart, "Let me burn out for God." In a few astonishing years, before tuberculosis took him at thirty-one, he translated the New Testament into Hindustani (Urdu) and Persian, and oversaw work in Arabic, laboring with relentless intensity against failing health. He traveled to Persia to perfect his translation and to reason with Muslim scholars about Christ, bearing patient witness to the gospel among those who denied the Savior. He died alone, far from home, at Tokat in Turkey, his work of translation a lasting gift to the church in the East. Martyn stands in the dictionary as the scholar who burned out for God, who poured the full strength of a brilliant mind and a frail body into giving the Word of Christ to the nations, and whose few years of total consecration have inspired generations to spend themselves wholly for the gospel.
webster_summary: English missionary and Bible translator (1781-1812) to India and Persia; a brilliant Cambridge scholar who resolved to "burn out for God," translated the New Testament into Urdu and Persian, and died at thirty-one.

corruption_paragraphs: Half-heartedness correction. The natural instinct is to spare ourselves, to hold back our gifts and strength for our own comfort and security. Martyn poured himself out without reserve, content to "burn out for God." The dictionary holds the apostolic spirit, "I will very gladly spend and be spent" (2 Cor 12:15); the servant of Christ is called not to preserve his life but to lose it for the gospel's sake (Mark 8:35), spending his all on the One who spent His all for him.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the urgency of the work while it is day. Martyn labored as a man who knew the night was coming, when no man can work (John 9:4), and crowded a lifetime of translation into a few brief years. The dictionary commends his urgency against a complacent delay: the day of opportunity is short, the nations still wait for the Word, and the faithful must work the works of Him that sent them while the light remains.

etymology: English missionary to China (1832-1905), founder of the China Inland Mission and pioneer of faith missions.
biblical_def: James Hudson Taylor was an English missionary to China and the founder of the China Inland Mission, one of the most influential figures in the history of modern missions. Convinced that the gospel must reach not only the coastal cities but the vast unreached interior of China, he founded in 1865 a mission marked by radical principles: missionaries would adopt Chinese dress and customs to remove needless barriers; the mission would go to the inland provinces no one else had reached; and it would operate by faith, making its needs known to God alone and never soliciting funds or going into debt. Taylor's watchword was that "God's work, done in God's way, will never lack God's supply." Through decades of labor, sickness, bereavement, and the martyrdom of many of his workers, the mission he founded brought hundreds of missionaries and the gospel deep into China, and its faith-principles shaped missions worldwide. Taylor stands in the dictionary as the pioneer of inland China and faith missions, who taught the church to trust God for the supply of His own work, to remove every needless barrier to the gospel, and to count the unreached interior worth a life of sacrifice and prayer.
webster_summary: English missionary to China (1832-1905), founder of the China Inland Mission and pioneer of faith missions; who took the gospel to the unreached interior and trusted God alone for supply: "God's work, done in God's way, will never lack God's supply."

corruption_summary: Taylor's life honors the recovery of faith in God's provision and the removal of needless cultural barriers to the gospel, against both a faithless reliance on human means and a refusal to become all things to all men for the lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Means-over-faith correction. The work of God is often reduced to fundraising and human strategy, as though its success depended on the techniques of men. Taylor's faith principles recovered a deeper truth: God's work done in God's way will never lack God's supply (Phil 4:19). The dictionary commends his confidence: the Lord who commands the mission also provides for it, and the church may labor for the unreached in dependence on the God who supplies all need according to His riches in glory.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is becoming all things to all men to save some. Taylor scandalized fellow missionaries by adopting Chinese dress and customs, refusing to let needless cultural barriers obscure the gospel. The dictionary holds the apostolic pattern (1 Cor 9:22): without compromising the truth, the missionary removes every avoidable offense, becoming weak to the weak, that by all means he might save some, and the gospel might reach the inland millions.

etymology: Scottish missionary (1824-1907) to the cannibal islands of the New Hebrides (Vanuatu).
biblical_def: John Gibson Paton was a Scottish missionary to the New Hebrides, a group of South Pacific islands then inhabited by cannibal peoples. Warned that he would be eaten by the natives, he famously replied that it made little difference whether he was consumed by cannibals or by worms, if he could but live and die serving Christ. Landing on the island of Tanna in 1858, he buried his young wife and infant son within months, digging their graves with his own hands and, as he wrote, would have gone mad beside that lonely grave but for the presence of Christ. He labored for years amid constant danger, hostility, and the deaths of fellow workers, before God opened the way; on the island of Aniwa he eventually saw nearly the whole population turn from heathen darkness to faith in Christ. His autobiography became a missionary classic. Paton stands in the dictionary as the dauntless missionary to the cannibal isles, who counted his life nothing for the sake of the gospel, who found Christ a sufficient companion beside the loneliest grave, and whose perseverance turned an island of darkness into a people who worship the living God.

corruption_summary: Paton's life honors the recovery of courageous, sacrificial missions and the sufficiency of Christ's presence in suffering, against a religion that counts its own life too dear to spend for the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-preservation correction. A comfortable Christianity counts its own safety too precious to risk for the lost. Paton, warned he would be eaten by cannibals, went anyway, counting not his life dear unto himself that he might finish his course and testify the gospel (Acts 20:24). The dictionary holds that the Great Commission is worth the risk of life; the missionary who loves his own comfort more than the perishing has not yet learned the worth of a soul or the command of Christ.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Christ's presence in the deepest sorrow. Beside the lonely grave of his wife and child, Paton testified that he would have lost his mind but for the abiding presence of Jesus, who promised never to leave nor forsake (Heb 13:5). The dictionary commends this comfort: the Lord who sends His servants to the ends of the earth goes with them, and is enough, even at the graveside in a hostile land.

etymology: Scottish missionary (1795-1883) to southern Africa, translator of the Setswana Bible and father-in-law of David Livingstone.
biblical_def: Robert Moffat was a Scottish missionary to southern Africa, a pioneer of the gospel among the Tswana people and one of the most significant missionaries of the nineteenth century. Beginning a gardener with little formal education, he gave more than fifty years to Africa, settling at Kuruman, where he built a mission station that became a base for the evangelization of the interior. After long and discouraging years, he saw a true work of God among the Tswana. His greatest labor was the translation of the entire Bible into Setswana, the first complete Bible in a southern African language, which he set in type and printed himself. His vivid accounts of the vast unreached interior, with its "smoke of a thousand villages" where Christ had never been named, stirred the young David Livingstone, who became Moffat's son-in-law and carried the gospel yet deeper into Africa. Moffat stands in the dictionary as the patient pioneer of the gospel in southern Africa, who gave the Tswana the Scriptures in their own tongue, who labored decades for a harvest he long could not see, and whose vision of the unreached interior sent others farther still.

Moffat counted the translation and printing of the Setswana Bible his crowning work, that the Tswana might read the wonders of God in their mother tongue. The dictionary commends the labor: the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD (Hab 2:14), and that knowledge comes as the Word is carried, translated, and printed for peoples who have never heard.

etymology: English Puritan missionary (1604-1690) in colonial Massachusetts, the "Apostle to the Indians," translator of the first Bible printed in America.
biblical_def: John Eliot was an English Puritan minister in colonial Massachusetts, remembered as the "Apostle to the Indians" for his pioneering labors among the Algonquin-speaking native peoples of New England. Settled as a pastor at Roxbury, he was gripped by a burden for the conversion of the Indians, learned their difficult language, and began to preach the gospel to them in their own tongue. He gathered converts into "praying towns," ordered Christian communities where the Indians might live under the Word of God. His monumental achievement was the translation of the entire Bible into the Massachusett (Algonquin) language — the first complete Bible printed in the American colonies, a labor of immense difficulty in a tongue that had never been written. Eliot also catechized, trained native preachers, and wrote works to aid the mission. Though the praying towns suffered grievously in later colonial wars, Eliot's labors stand as the first great Protestant mission to the native peoples of America. He stands in the dictionary as the Apostle to the Indians, who gave his strength to learn a hard language and render the whole Scripture into it, that the native peoples of the New World might read the wonderful works of God in their own tongue.
webster_summary: English Puritan missionary (1604-1690) in colonial Massachusetts, the "Apostle to the Indians"; who gathered native converts into "praying towns" and translated the entire Bible into Algonquin, the first Bible printed in America.

The dictionary holds the breadth of the Great Commission: every kindred, tongue, people, and nation (Rev 5:9) is to hear, including those near at hand, and the church is bound to bring the Word to the peoples among whom God has placed it.

The dictionary commends the work of Bible translation as essential to missions: faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God (Rom 10:17), so the Word must be carried into every language under heaven.

etymology: English missionary (1782-1834), the first Protestant missionary to China and translator of the first Chinese Bible.
biblical_def: Robert Morrison was an English missionary, the first Protestant missionary to China, who against enormous obstacles laid the foundation for the evangelization of the world's most populous nation. Arriving in 1807, he found China closed to missionaries and the teaching of Chinese to foreigners forbidden on pain of death; he labored in secret, in poor health and deep isolation, learning the language and working as a translator for a trading company to remain in the country. Over years of patient toil he produced the first translation of the whole Bible into Chinese and compiled a massive Chinese-English dictionary that served generations of missionaries and scholars after him. In twenty-seven years he saw only a handful of converts, yet he had given China the Scriptures and the tools to learn its language, sowing seed that would yield a vast harvest long after his death. Morrison stands in the dictionary as the first Protestant missionary to China and translator of its first Bible, who labored in obscurity and discouragement for a harvest he would not live to see, trusting that the Word of God given to a people would not return void though the day of reaping be far off.
webster_summary: English missionary (1782-1834), the first Protestant missionary to China; who labored in secret against a closed empire, translated the first Chinese Bible, and compiled a Chinese-English dictionary, sowing seed for a harvest far beyond his own few converts.

corruption_summary: Morrison's life honors the recovery of patient labor that sows for harvests beyond one's own lifetime, against a results-obsessed age that measures faithfulness by immediate success.
corruption_paragraphs: Immediate-results correction. A success-driven mindset judges a labor worthless if it does not quickly produce visible fruit. Morrison gave twenty-seven years to China and saw only a handful of converts, yet he had given the nation its first Bible. The dictionary holds that faithfulness, not immediate harvest, is the measure of the servant: one plants, another waters, but God gives the increase (1 Cor 3:6), often long after the sower is gone. The vast Chinese church of later ages grew from seed Morrison sowed in tears.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is sowing in hope of a distant reaping. Morrison cast his bread upon the waters, trusting to find it after many days (Eccl 11:1), and did not grow weary in well-doing though he reaped little himself. The dictionary commends his faith: the Word of God does not return void (Isa 55:11), and the labor of the faithful, though it seem barren in their own day, will yield in due season a harvest that vindicates every tear.
roots_summary: English missionary (1782-1834), the first Protestant missionary to China; who translated the first Chinese Bible and sowed seed for a harvest far beyond his own few converts.

Arrived in 1807 to a China closed to missionaries
Labored in secret, learning a forbidden language

usage: Robert Morrison — first Protestant missionary to China and translator of its first Bible.
My word... shall not return unto me void (Isa 55:11) — Morrison's confidence in the seed he sowed.
Morrison saw few converts, yet gave China the Scriptures for a harvest beyond his lifetime.

etymology: Irish missionary (1867-1951) to India, founder of the Dohnavur Fellowship and rescuer of endangered children.
biblical_def: Amy Carmichael was an Irish missionary to India who gave fifty-five years of unbroken service, never once returning home on furlough, and who founded the Dohnavur Fellowship in south India as a refuge for children in danger. Burdened by the plight of young girls (and later boys) being given to Hindu temples for ritual prostitution, she labored at great risk to rescue them, gathering hundreds of children into a Christian family at Dohnavur where they were raised in the love of Christ. She bore the work's burdens as a spiritual mother, and after an injury spent her last twenty years largely confined to bed, from which she wrote many devotional books, including If, a searching meditation on the marks of Calvary love, and Gold by Moonlight. Her writings, marked by deep devotion to Christ crucified and a refusal of self-pity, have fed the church far beyond India. Carmichael stands in the dictionary as the rescuer of endangered children and a writer of Calvary love, who poured out a long life without reserve for the least and most vulnerable, and who taught the church that the love which counts no cost is the love that was shown at the cross.
webster_summary: Irish missionary (1867-1951) to India, founder of the Dohnavur Fellowship; who rescued hundreds of children from temple prostitution, served fifty-five years without furlough, and wrote devotional classics like If on Calvary love.

Founder of the Dohnavur Fellowship in south India.
Rescued hundreds of children from temple prostitution and danger.
Served fifty-five years in India without a single furlough home.
Author of devotional classics including If, on the marks of Calvary love.

corruption_summary: Carmichael's life honors the recovery of self-sacrificing love for the vulnerable and the cross-shaped love that counts no cost, against a sentimental religion that loves in word but not in deed.
corruption_paragraphs: Love-in-word correction. It is easy to profess compassion and never pay its cost. Carmichael's love was costly and concrete: she risked everything to rescue endangered children and gave a long life to raising them, refusing even the relief of furlough. The dictionary holds that real love lays down its life for others, as Christ laid down His for us (1 John 3:16); pure religion visits the fatherless in their affliction (James 1:27), and the love that costs nothing is not the love of Calvary.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the seriousness with which Christ regards the little ones. Carmichael took to heart the Lord's warning that to offend one of these little ones invites a millstone (Matt 18:6), and the promise that to receive a child in His name is to receive Him (Matt 18:5). The dictionary commends her example: care for the most vulnerable is not a sentimental add-on to the faith but near the heart of it, for in the least of these we serve the Lord Himself.

etymology: American missionary (1927-1956) martyred with four companions by the Waorani people of Ecuador.
biblical_def: Jim Elliot was an American missionary to Ecuador, one of five young men martyred in 1956 in an attempt to bring the gospel to the Waorani (then called Auca), an isolated and violent people of the Ecuadorian rainforest. A man of fervent devotion from his college years, he had written in his journal the words that became his epitaph and a watchword for missions: "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose." With Nate Saint, Ed McCully, Peter Fleming, and Roger Youderian, he made contact with the Waorani and was speared to death on a sandbar of the Curaray River, the five men choosing not to use their guns against those they had come to save. Their deaths, far from ending the mission, stirred a wave of missionary commitment around the world; and through the continued labors of Elliot's widow Elisabeth and Nate Saint's sister Rachel, many of the very people who killed them came to faith in Christ. Elliot stands in the dictionary as a martyr of the modern missionary movement, whose surrender of all he could not keep, to gain what he could not lose, has called a generation to count their lives nothing for the sake of reaching the unreached with the gospel.
webster_summary: American missionary (1927-1956) martyred with four companions by the Waorani of Ecuador; whose journal words, "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose," and whose death stirred a generation to missions.
webster_full: JIM ELLIOT, proper noun. American missionary (1927-1956) to Ecuador.

Phil 3:8

corruption_summary: Elliot's life honors the recovery of the eternal calculus of discipleship — spending what cannot be kept to gain what cannot be lost — against a worldly wisdom that hoards this life and counts such sacrifice insane.
corruption_paragraphs: Worldly-wisdom correction. The world counts it madness to risk one's life to reach a hostile and obscure people. Elliot reckoned by an eternal arithmetic: "He is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose." The dictionary holds the Savior's own logic: what shall it profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his soul (Mark 8:36)? The believer who spends his perishable life for Christ's imperishable kingdom has made the wisest of all exchanges.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is overcoming by not loving one's life unto death. Elliot and his companions died as the martyrs of old, who overcame by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony, loving not their lives unto the death (Rev 12:11). The dictionary commends their witness: the seed of the church is the blood of the martyrs, and the death of these five young men, far from defeat, became a summons that sent a generation to the ends of the earth.
